content: Inhalation of hypertonic saline has been shown to improve the physical properties of sputum, enhance mucociliary clearance, and lead to better clinical outcomes in individuals with cystic fibrosis. This study aimed to evaluate whether the timing of hypertonic saline inhalation, either in relation to airway clearance techniques or the time of day, affects its clinical efficacy. The researchers conducted a systematic search for randomized and quasi-randomized controlled trials using the Cochrane Cystic Fibrosis Trials Register, the Physiotherapy Evidence Database (PEDro), and international cystic fibrosis conference proceedings. The last search was performed on February 28, 2019. The inclusion criteria required studies to randomize participants based on the timing of hypertonic saline inhalation, such as inhalation up to six hours before, during, or up to six hours after airway clearance techniques, or morning versus evening inhalation. Out of 104 trial reports identified, 51 trials were reviewed, and three cross-over trials involving 77 participants met the inclusion criteria. These trials compared three timing regimens: inhalation before versus during airway clearance techniques, inhalation before versus after airway clearance techniques, and inhalation during versus after airway clearance techniques. One trial with 50 participants included all three comparisons due to its three-arm design. No trials compared morning versus evening inhalation. The evidence from these trials was rated as low quality due to limitations such as high risk of bias from lack of blinding and indirectness, as all participants were adults, making the findings less applicable to children. The intervention periods were short, ranging from one to three treatments in a single day. The results showed no clinically significant differences in lung function or symptom scores between the timing regimens of inhaling hypertonic saline before, during, or after airway clearance techniques. The between-group comparisons were not statistically significant. Satisfaction ratings were similar when hypertonic saline was inhaled before versus during airway clearance techniques. However, satisfaction appeared to be lower when inhalation occurred after airway clearance techniques compared to before (mean difference [MD] 20.38 mm, 95% confidence interval [CI] 12.10 to 28.66) or during (MD 14.80 mm, 95% CI 5.70 to 23.90) on a 100-mm scale. Perceived effectiveness followed a similar pattern. There was little or no difference between inhalation before versus during airway clearance techniques. However, perceived effectiveness was lower when inhalation occurred after airway clearance techniques compared to before (MD 10.62, 95% CI 2.54 to 18.70) or during (MD 15.60, 95% CI 7.55 to 23.65). None of the trials reported data on quality of life or adverse events. The authors concluded that the timing of hypertonic saline inhalation has little or no impact on lung function, based on low-certainty evidence. However, inhaling hypertonic saline before or during airway clearance techniques may enhance perceived efficacy and satisfaction. The long-term benefits of hypertonic saline have been established for twice-daily inhalations, but if only one dose per day is feasible, the timing could be based on convenience or tolerability until further evidence becomes available. The trials reviewed were of very short duration, and longer-term studies are needed to assess the effects of regular use, including adherence over time and potential adverse effects associated with prolonged use.
